claims.text: The starting powder is an equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi mixture, corresponding to 20 at.% of each element.
The elemental powders may contain surface oxide layers.
Mechanical alloying followed by SPS can consolidate a high-entropy alloy from elemental or mechanically alloyed powders.
High-energy milling creates severe plastic deformation, a high dislocation density, and nanoscale elemental mixing in CoCrFeNiTi.
Stored deformation energy from milling drives diffusion and grain-boundary migration during SPS.
Heating at 100°C/min and holding for 5 minutes at 950°C kinetically suppresses nucleation and growth of a Ti-rich HCP phase.
The same rapid SPS cycle provides sufficient diffusion to form a metastable FCC/BCC solid solution.
A uniaxial pressure of 60 MPa closes pores and enhances pressure-assisted atomic diffusion.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between Ti and the other elements produces a high initial sintering strain rate and local stresses that stabilize FCC against transformation to HCP.
The proposed process will produce greater than 98% theoretical density.
The proposed process will produce a grain size of approximately 50–100 nm.
The resulting CoCrFeNiTi alloy will be dominated by FCC with a minor BCC phase.
The resulting alloy will have a Vickers hardness of 450–550 HV.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries can contribute to elevated hardness through grain-boundary strengthening.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi is porous, coarse-grained, single-phase FCC, and has a hardness of approximately 150–200 HV.
SPS temperatures below 850°C provide insufficient diffusion, whereas temperatures above 1050°C cause grain coarsening and HCP precipitation.
Prolonged milling can introduce carbide or oxide contamination even when a protective atmosphere is used.
Titanium additions can increase hardness, strength, and wear resistance in high-entropy alloys.
At 20 at.% Ti, local HCP nucleation may still occur at grain boundaries and cause localized brittleness.
SPS at 1100°C is expected to cause both grain growth and HCP formation in CoCrFeNiTi.

contradictions.description: The experiment is intended to falsify the claim that hardness arises from grain refinement rather than Ti solute strengthening, but it declares statistically equal hardness in Ti-containing CoCrFeNiTi and Ti-free CoCrFeNi to be falsifying. Such equality would instead indicate that Ti solute strengthening is negligible and would therefore be consistent with, rather than contrary to, a grain-refinement explanation.
